title: The journey of a returnable cup
content:
Returnable takeaway cups offer a simple image of a circular system: a customer receives a drink, returns the cup and allows it to be used again. In practice, the environmental outcome depends on a sequence of less visible actions. A cup must reach a collection point, survive handling, be washed effectively and return to a place where it can replace a disposable one. A district-wide trial therefore focused on the organisation of reuse rather than on promoting a particular material. The organisers wanted to know which arrangements kept cups moving through the system, not merely whether customers liked the idea.

Several independent cafés joined the trial. Customers paid a deposit that was refunded when they returned a cup to any participating café, regardless of where the drink had been bought. This shared return rule was intended to make returning a cup compatible with an ordinary journey. It also created an imbalance: a café near a transport stop received many returns but sold comparatively few drinks in returnable cups. Counting only sales would have hidden its contribution and the work involved. The organisers arranged collections according to the accumulation of cups rather than dividing visits equally among the cafés.

A washing contractor offered capacity on a route already serving local businesses. Using that route avoided creating a separate journey for every small batch, but it did not make transport irrelevant. An unscheduled collection could still require additional travel, and clean cups sometimes waited at the depot because cafés had not ordered replacements in time. The system needed a way to anticipate demand as well as remove used cups. A full collection bin and an empty cupboard could occur at the same café: one indicated successful returns, while the other could force staff to hand out disposable cups.

The organisers recorded the number of times each marked cup completed a return-and-wash cycle. They also counted cups withdrawn because they were damaged or permanently stained. A high return rate was encouraging, but it did not guarantee a long working life. Conversely, a robust cup that remained in a customer's kitchen was physically intact without contributing another use. The useful measure was the number of actual cycles, considered alongside losses and washing requirements. Choosing a durable material mattered, but durability could not compensate for a collection system that failed to recover it.

Customers were invited to comment at the cafés and through a short online form. Many comments concerned convenience rather than environmental claims. A larger deposit was suggested as a way to encourage returns, yet the organisers were cautious: it could also discourage a first purchase by customers with little spare cash. They retained the existing deposit during the trial rather than changing several parts of the scheme at once. This decision left the effect of a larger deposit unresolved. Positive comments about reuse were not interpreted as proof that customers would accept any price or level of inconvenience.

For the final evaluation, the organisers compared the observed system with plausible alternatives. A returned cup did not always replace a disposable cup; some customers would otherwise have brought their own. The washing equipment's energy use also varied with how fully it was loaded. Instead of publishing a single saving for every drink, the report showed how the conclusion changed under different assumptions about replacement, transport and washing. This made the message less convenient for a poster but more useful for deciding where the scheme could improve.

The trial ended with a recommendation to expand the network gradually while monitoring collection points and stock. The cafés had shown that a shared scheme could operate, but the report distinguished that operational finding from a universal environmental claim. A different district might have longer journeys, fewer participating shops or less suitable washing capacity. The lesson was to examine the whole route through which a cup becomes available for another use. Reuse is an achievement of that route, not a property that a container acquires simply by being labelled returnable.

questions.question: What was the trial primarily designed to investigate?
options: A. Which cup material customers found most attractive
B. Whether environmental advertising increased drink sales
C. How reuse could be organised in everyday operation
D. Whether every customer supported a deposit
questions.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
questions.evidence: The organisers wanted to know which arrangements kept cups moving through the system, not merely whether customers liked the idea.
questions.explanation: The organisers investigated the arrangements that kept cups circulating.
questions.trap: A true detail from a different part of the process may not answer the question asked.
questions.tip: Locate the supporting sentence, compare the complete meaning and check the answer instructions.

analysis.keyEvidence: which arrangements kept cups moving through the system

optionReasons.A: No comparison of material appearance is described.
optionReasons.B: The trial concerned organisation, not an advertising experiment.
optionReasons.C: The organisers investigated the arrangements that kept cups circulating.
optionReasons.D: Customers’ opinions were collected, but universal deposit support was not the central question.

B. The return workload was unevenly distributed

D. Customers could only return cups where they bought drinks

questions.question: Which TWO limitations of judging success from returns or durability alone are identified?
options: A. Durable materials cannot be washed
B. A returned cup can still have a short working life
C. Cup markings always disappear after washing
D. Keeping a cup at home was prohibited
E. An intact cup may never complete another use
questions.evidence: A high return rate was encouraging, but it did not guarantee a long working life. Conversely, a robust cup that remained in a customer's kitchen was physically intact without contributing another use.
questions.explanation: B is supported by the possibility of withdrawal after return; E is supported by an intact cup remaining in a customer’s kitchen.
questions.trap: Do not substitute manufacturing claims or a supposed ban on home use for the stated limits.

optionReasons.A: No inability to wash durable materials is stated.
optionReasons.B: Correct: returning does not prevent damage or staining from ending a cup’s working life.

optionReasons.D: The text describes cups kept at home but states no prohibition.
optionReasons.E: Correct: a robust cup in a customer’s kitchen remains intact without contributing another use.
